paragraphs.heading: Telling light apart
paragraphs.text: Color vision is the ability to tell apart light made of different frequencies, whatever its brightness. It begins when light entering the eye stirs different types of photoreceptors, the eye's light-sensing cells, by different amounts. Their signals then travel through many layers of nerve cells and end up feeding higher functions of the brain.

paragraphs.heading: The visible spectrum
paragraphs.text: Isaac Newton found that white light, once split into its colors by one prism, could be joined back into white light by a second prism. The light we can see spans roughly 380 to 740 nanometers in wavelength. Each spectral color covers a band, not a single wavelength: red runs from 625 to 740 nm, green from 500 to 565 nm, and violet from 380 to 450 nm. Longer wavelengths are called infrared and shorter ones ultraviolet. People generally cannot see them, but some other animals may.

paragraphs.heading: Rods for night, cones for day
paragraphs.text: In very dim light, vision is scotopic: rod cells in the retina pick up the light. Rods respond best near 500 nm and do little or nothing for color. In bright light such as daylight, vision is photopic: cone cells take over, and they are what give us color, responding best near 555 nm. In between, in mesopic vision, rods and cones both send signals. The change in how colors look as light goes from dim to bright is called the Purkinje effect.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds of cone
paragraphs.text: Color perception starts in the cones. Each cone holds a form of opsin, a pigment protein, and the different forms respond to different ranges of wavelength. Humans have three types, which makes our color vision trichromatic. By the order of their peak wavelengths they are labelled short (S), medium (M) and long (L).

paragraphs.heading: Not really red, green and blue
paragraphs.text: The three cone types do not line up neatly with the colors we name. L cones are often called red receptors, yet measurements show they respond most in the greenish-yellow part of the spectrum, and S and M cones are not simply blue and green either. So the RGB color model is a handy way to represent color, not a copy of the eye's cones. Color perception starts from the differing outputs of the cones in the retina, and the process is finished in the brain's visual cortex and its associative areas. Two complementary theories describe it: the trichromatic theory and the opponent process theory.

paragraphs.heading: Colors beyond the rainbow
paragraphs.text: Many colors we see are not in the spectrum at all. Pink comes from mixing red with white, brown from orange with gray or black, and navy from blue with black. The spectrum is a line with violet at one end and red at the other, yet we see purples that join the two ends. White can come from the full spectrum or, in humans, from red, green and blue together, or just a complementary pair such as blue and yellow.

paragraphs.heading: Impossible colors
paragraphs.text: Some combinations of cone responses can never come about naturally; the colors they would give are called impossible colors. For example, the medium cones cannot be switched on fully by themselves. If they could, we would see a 'hyper-green' color.

paragraphs.heading: Why color vision evolved
paragraphs.text: Many animals see color, using similar mechanisms built from the same kinds of biological molecules. In primates, color vision may have evolved to help with tasks such as finding nutritious young leaves, ripe fruit and flowers, spotting camouflaged predators, and reading emotions in other primates. Even among people with typical color vision, the peak responses of the cones differ from person to person.
